The Earth observation network, which relies heavily on satellite data, offers significant benefits for both our planet and its inhabitants. The increasing number of satellites in orbit, including both commercial and non-commercial options, presents a complex challenge for those seeking to access and utilize this data. The emergence of the satellite industry has led to a shift from public data towards a subscription-based model, limiting its potential use in areas such as climate change and disaster relief. In response to this challenge, we have developed a novel satellite data platform called EarthNets, which leverages the capabilities of blockchain technology to provide a global network of interconnected satellites. By doing so, we aim to provide a secure, fair, and data-rich environment that benefits a wide range of stakeholders, including satellite operators, researchers, and the general public. The platform's architecture is designed to ensure fair data sharing, and we have also developed a data pricing mechanism that rewards satellite operators for their contributions, thereby promoting a collaborative and sustainable approach to satellite-based data provision. In this paper, we present our initial research on EarthNets, a blockchain-based platform that enables a fair, open, and data-rich Earth observation ecosystem. The platform's potential applications are vast, including climate change mitigation, disaster relief, and environmental conservation. Specifically, we demonstrate how our data pricing mechanism can support disaster relief efforts, and we also outline the potential for EarthNets to facilitate research in areas such as climate change and satellite-based remote sensing. In addition, we provide a roadmap outlining the key technical and business objectives for the next phase of our research. This research has been made possible through our collaboration with the Space Chain Alliance, a global organization dedicated to promoting a blockchain-based space industry. Deep learning techniques have gained significant attention for diagnosing brain tumors, particularly due to their potential to improve the accuracy of classification models. Recent advancements in 3D UNet architectures have shown promise in this area, but there remains a need to optimize their performance on brain tumor classification. This study introduces a novel 3D UNet design that incorporates context, leveraging encoder features to inform decoder predictions in a context-aware manner. By utilizing the encoder's feature maps as a context vector, this approach enables the model to capture the nuances of brain tumor data. We evaluate the proposed architecture on two benchmark datasets: the BraTS 2018 and the BraTS 2020. Our results demonstrate that the model achieves an impressive accuracy of 96.0\% on the latter dataset, outperforming the baseline. Furthermore, our model's performance on the BraTS 2018 dataset demonstrates a significant improvement over the baseline, with accuracy rates of 96.0\%, 96.2\%, and 96.1\% for the basic, weighted, and context-sensitive variants, respectively. These findings underscore the potential of our context-sensitive 3D UNet model for brain tumor classification. The performance of the approach is evaluated using a real-world example of influenza incidence data, and simulations are conducted to compare the results with existing methods. The findings suggest that the proposed approach offers a reliable and computationally efficient solution for large-scale modeling applications. The rapid expansion of visual content across the web has led to the creation of massive datasets, which are difficult to manage and analyze. To address this issue, a new standard called SPARQL was introduced to facilitate data querying among web applications. Although SPARQL excels in handling structured data, it falls short in processing visual content. To bridge this gap, a new language called Visual SPARQL (VGStore) has been developed. By integrating visual scene graphs with RDF data models, VGStore enables the interrogation of multimodal data, including object recognition, relationship analysis, and data filtering. Through experiments and evaluations, it has been demonstrated that VGStore outperforms SPARQL in terms of scene graph filtering and multimodal data retrieval. In computer vision, filters are a crucial component of CNNs, but their overabundance can lead to inefficiencies. To mitigate this, reducing the number of filters while maintaining network performance is essential. Our research introduces a novel approach by decomposing filters using self-affinity matrix analysis. By leveraging this technique, we can efficiently reduce filters without compromising CNN functionality. Our method is adaptable to various filter types and can be applied to different network layers. We have successfully implemented thinning filters in well-known CNNs, including VGG16, ResNet34, and EfficientNetB0. When compared to other filter thinning techniques, our approach yields superior results. When evaluated on the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets, our method achieved a 0.35% improvement in accuracy compared to the original networks. Furthermore, our implementation on the CIFAR10 dataset demonstrates a 12.5% reduction in FLOPs and 14.1% decrease in latency, as well as a 1.5% accuracy improvement. Deep neural networks often struggle with inaccurate or unreliable predictions due to the issue of inaccurate feature learning. This problem is particularly evident in datasets with interconnected classes, where neural networks may mistakenly identify features that are specific to one class as being relevant to another. In order to address this limitation, we developed a novel training approach called In-Training Representation Synchronization (IRIS). IRIS achieves reliable feature learning by synchronizing the hidden representations of the network during training, thereby forcing the network to produce coherent and consistent features. Unlike previous methods that rely on external regularization or modifications to the loss function, IRIS integrates feature learning into the standard end-to-end neural network training process. This approach eliminates the need for manual parameter tuning and significantly improves prediction accuracy. Furthermore, IRIS can be seamlessly integrated into existing neural networks without modifying their architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that IRIS can achieve state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, including image recognition, speech recognition, and text classification. For instance, IRIS achieved a 7% improvement in accuracy on the MNIST dataset, a 4% improvement on the Speech Command dataset, and a 3% improvement on the AGNews dataset. Language learning through interactive technology has proven to be highly effective.
Despite this, there is a lack of natural language tasks specifically designed for native language learners of English. 
This study introduces SC-Ques, a new dataset consisting of phrase completion questions, which simulates how native speakers of English ask questions and assesses English proficiency. 
SC-Qes was created using real-world data from English speakers and pre-qualified by expert judges, resulting in a reliable resource for evaluating native language learners' proficiency in English. 
The dataset was also tested by various AI models, which showed that while they performed well on easier tasks, they struggled with more complex ones. 
This study's findings can serve as a benchmark for the development of AI models tailored to native language learners' needs and abilities. 
The data and code for SC-Qes are available at https://github.com/zhuyi92/SC-Ques. 
A video demonstrating the dataset can be found at https://youtu.be/7qzqzqzqzqz. 
The study's results were also presented at the 60th annual meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics in 2022.

Current datasets for evaluating image quality have limitations, primarily focusing on day-light images. However, these datasets may not accurately reflect real-world camera performance in low-light conditions. Recent breakthroughs in adversarial training have significantly improved the resilience of models against subtle attacks. However, most methods are ineffective against sophisticated and tailored attacks that target vulnerabilities in specific areas of the model's map. This study presents a novel adversarial training approach, dubbed Latent Frontier (Ladder), which enhances the model's robustness to sophisticated and easier-to-eradicate attacks. Ladder achieves this by leveraging a modified version of the model's map, derived from the model's decision boundary, to identify and prioritize the model's most vulnerable areas. Furthermore, we propose a training objective that forces the model to recognize and differentiate between different levels of attack severity, thereby increasing its ability to detect and respond to both simple and complex attacks. Thorough experiments across multiple datasets have demonstrated that Ladder surpasses existing methods in improving both the model's ability to detect and resist both simple and sophisticated attacks. Additionally, we provide theoretical evidence to support the effectiveness of Ladder in mitigating the impact of both straightforward and sophisticated attacks. The code for Ladder is available on GitHub. For more information, please visit the project's website. https://sites.google.com/view/ladder-adv.

The task of categorizing bird types is a complex and challenging problem due to the vast number of species, which often exhibit nearly identical visual characteristics. This research aims to develop a system for identifying bird types from a given image, which can be a useful application in ornithological research and conservation efforts. However, the task is complicated by the vast number of species, which makes it difficult to collect a comprehensive dataset. To address this issue, the authors propose a novel approach that leverages transfer learning and multistage training. This approach involves training a model on a large dataset of images from bird-related Wikipedia pages, which includes a diverse set of bird types. The model is then fine-tuned using a smaller dataset of images from the iNaturalist platform. The authors also employ data augmentation techniques to enhance the training data and utilize class activation maps to provide a visual explanation of the model's predictions. The proposed approach achieved an impressive accuracy of 85.4% on the iNaturalist test set. The authors also conducted an in-depth analysis of the model's performance on various bird types and examined the visual characteristics that the model learned from the bird-related Wikipedia images. To facilitate further research, the authors have released a comprehensive dataset and code for the iNaturalist 2021 Birds challenge. Our research focuses on the issue of cache side channels in software, which allows data extraction through cache faults caused by indirect CPU operations. This phenomenon has been proven to be exploitable in various studies. To address this problem, we have developed an innovative method called CacheQL that enables the detection of cache side channels in software. This method involves creating a specialized database to track the cache side channels in a given program. This tool allows for both the identification of potential vulnerabilities in software and the precise location of the specific lines that are vulnerable to such attacks. This technology has been successfully tested on a range of real-world applications, including a specific analysis of the Python programming language. This analysis revealed that the Python standard library is susceptible to cache side channels in software, which led to the identification of multiple vulnerabilities in widely used libraries. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in quickly identifying cache side channel vulnerabilities in software, even in complex production software, and provides a clear path for further improvement in this area. This research focuses on developing autonomous, distributed control systems for a quadruped robot to achieve formation tracking with a bearing-only guidance. The main achievement of this study is designing sliding-mode controllers that enable the robot to track formations using limited directional information, such as bearing measurements. The proposed controllers do not rely on prior knowledge of the robot's workspace or its physical characteristics, only requiring knowledge of its neighbors. The research also presents a decentralized estimation algorithm to determine initial conditions for the sliding-mode controllers and demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through simulations of various scenarios involving up to 100 quadruped robots. The results show that the proposed controller achieves stable formation tracking with high accuracy and minimal tracking errors, even in the presence of significant disturbances and with a computational complexity of O(n) operations. The availability of open-source code facilitates its implementation. The underlying algorithms are grounded in mathematical principles and provide a rigorous foundation for their analysis. The research also includes a comparative analysis of the proposed solution with alternative approaches, highlighting its advantages and limitations. Ultimately, this study contributes to the development of bearing-only guidance systems for multi-robot coordination and contributes to the broader field of control systems research. To model the complex relationships between various aspects of a population, it is essential to consider the multiple layers of these connections. This is particularly relevant in the study of brain networks, where accurate representation is crucial for understanding the structure of the brain. This paper introduces a new method, MultiSAGE, which uses a random walk-based approach to predict the connections between populations based on their individual characteristics. By applying this method to various datasets, we demonstrate its effectiveness in population-to-population prediction, as well as its ability to identify specific relationships between populations. Furthermore, our results show that MultiSAGE outperforms other methods, such as a simplified version of SAGE, in predicting population interactions. We also observe that certain brain regions are more influential than others in these predictions. Overall, our findings suggest that MultiSAGE is a valuable tool for understanding the structure of the brain. This research has important implications for understanding the structure of the brain and may shed light on the mechanisms underlying various neurological disorders. The primary goal of dehazing is to restore clear images by removing haze-induced distortions.
Recent advancements in dehazing algorithms have been extensively documented.
However, evaluating the quality of dehazed images remains a significant challenge due to the subjective nature of human perception and the scarcity of reliable quality metrics.
This paper presents a novel metric for assessing dehazed image quality based on the analysis of spatial frequency components.
By leveraging the concept of partial divergence, our approach incorporates domain-specific knowledge to evaluate dehazed images.

Additionally, this work provides insights into the characteristics of dehazed images and identifies areas for further improvement in future dehazing research. In this study, we introduce a novel approach, called IDP, which leverages a two-step process involving a model-driven step and picture-based learning to effectively remove haze from individual images. By formulating the haze effect as an algebraic equation, we can derive a set of meaningful parameters from a single hazy image. These parameters serve as input features to train a neural network using a large dataset of dehazed images. By combining the features extracted from the neural network with a model-driven approach, we can generate a realistic and clear dehazed image. Furthermore, we also propose a new method for evaluating the quality of dehazed images, which takes into account both visual quality and semantic factors. Our experimental results demonstrate that IDP achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Deep learning models have become highly susceptible to sophisticated cyber-attacks. A particularly insidious form of cyber-attack involves an adversary manipulating a deep learning model's input to induce false predictions. To address this vulnerability, we introduce DeepPayload, a sophisticated tool that exploits machine learning models' weaknesses. DeepPayload employs a neural payload insertion framework, combining white-box and black-box methods to develop a tailored attack. This novel approach involves training a surrogate model to generate malicious input perturbations that successfully trigger false predictions. Using this technique, we successfully launched successful attacks on prominent models such as YOLOv5, BERT, and Densenet, by inserting custom payloads into input data. Our results show that these attacks produce highly accurate, high-fidelity false positives. Additionally, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, achieving a 90% attack success rate in a black-box setting. By releasing DeepPayload as an open-source tool, we aim to encourage researchers to advance the field of explainable adversarial machine learning and inform the development of practical cyber-defense strategies. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to significant improvements in predictive accuracy for survival outcomes. Notably, predictive models can be categorized into two types: probabilistic and non-probabilistic. Probabilistic models estimate the probability of surviving beyond a specified time frame, whereas non-probabilistic ones estimate hazard rates at a particular time. However, existing non-probabilistic models struggle to provide predictive distributions of future survival times. To address this limitation, we introduce the inverse survival model (RSM), a probabilistic model that estimates the probability of future survival times by modeling the inverse of the cumulative hazard rate. This model offers a clear advantage over existing non-probabilistic models and can be trained using gradient-based methods. Through simulations and case studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the RSM in predicting future survival times and show its superior performance over existing models. Moreover, our results indicate that RSMs can provide more accurate predictions than hazard rate models, especially when there are significant changes in the hazard rates over time. Additionally, our analysis reveals that RSMs can provide more accurate predictions than probabilistic models, especially when there are significant changes in the survival distributions over time. Overall, our study highlights the potential of the RSM as a powerful tool for predicting future survival times in medical applications. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, ensemble Q-learning is an approach that combines diverse strategies to prevent a single policy from deteriorating when faced with non-stationary environments. Although ensemble learning is beneficial, the diversity of individual components is not always guaranteed, resulting in suboptimal outcomes. The proposed approach is applied to a real-world multi-agent scenario and successfully demonstrates its effectiveness in improving representation diversity and overall performance. Notably, the introduction of additional rewards does not hinder the value function and, under certain conditions, can even accelerate learning. The results suggest that this approach can be a valuable tool for improving reinforcement learning algorithms in complex, dynamic environments. In a high-dimensional statistical context, we investigate the optimal rate of convergence for estimators under a high-dimensional linear functional model. We establish an upper bound on the disturbance direction's dimension and a corresponding rate of convergence based on this bound. This bound is both necessary and sufficient for achieving the optimal rate of convergence under a mild Gaussianity assumption. The resulting rate is particularly notable in low-dimensional disturbance settings, where it remains constant despite increasing dimensionality. We also explore the implications of our findings for statistical analysis of high-dimensional networks and multivariate time series data. Specifically, in the context of network estimation, we examine the influence of node degree on the estimation accuracy and derive conditions under which the disturbance dimension's upper bound can be relaxed. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of our methods in high-dimensional time series analysis and demonstrate their applicability in the analysis of functional data using the Indian summer monsoon rainfall data as an illustrative example. The organic search function on e-commerce websites enables users to browse products without the influence of recommended items. Research indicates that users value the order in which items are displayed in the search results, as it impacts their shopping decisions and user satisfaction. Presently, most e-commerce websites utilize a basic search algorithm that ranks items based on the relevance of keywords and user behavior. To enhance the user experience of organic search on e-commerce websites, this study proposes an innovative item ranking method called Page Generation (PGG). PPG leverages a deep neural network to generate item representations combining item information and user behavior, and then utilizes these representations to rank items according to user needs. Evaluations of PPG using real-world data from an e-commerce website show that it surpasses the performance of the current ranking method, resulting in a 9.38% increase in user satisfaction. Additionally, PPG has been successfully implemented in the real-world scenario of an e-commerce website, yielding a 10.11% boost in user satisfaction. The Transformer model has achieved significant success in handling sequential data, yet it is limited by its computational and memory-intensive nature. To address this limitation, researchers have introduced sparse attention mechanisms as a way to scale Transformers to larger sizes while improving their efficiency. However, these approaches often come with additional training and fine-tuning complexities. To overcome these challenges, a novel regularization method called Gating Dropout is proposed, allowing for more efficient regularization of pre-trained Transformers with improved performance and a lower computational cost. Gating Dropout is achieved by introducing a dropout mechanism directly into the attention gating mechanism, rather than modifying the pre-trained model. Through its application, it is possible to dynamically control the trade-off between model accuracy and computational and memory requirements. Experimental results demonstrate that Gating Dropout outperforms previous approaches, enabling a 2x reduction in computational and memory costs with minimal accuracy loss across various tasks, including natural language processing and computer vision. Moreover, it is shown that Gating Dropout can be used to achieve a 5x reduction in computational and memory costs while maintaining comparable accuracy to sparse attention approaches. Notably, it is possible to achieve a 50% reduction in computational and memory costs while maintaining 90% of the accuracy when compared to the baseline Transformer model. These findings make Gating Dropout a promising solution for efficiently training and fine-tuning large Transformers. We introduce NODE-CHOOSE, a graph neural network (GNN) that leverages a discriminative propagation technique to derive node representations. Unlike standard GNNs, NODE-CHOOSE's node representations are solely based on observed data, eliminating the need for an optimization step. The framework is designed to incorporate user-specified node features and generate representations for unobserved nodes, which can then be utilized in various tasks such as link prediction and node classification. Additionally, our framework is shown to be resilient to adversarial attacks and efficiently scalable to large networks. NODE-CHOOSE's source code is available for public use on GitHub. Furthermore, we introduce a novel dataset called Link Prediction under Unobserved Data, featuring nodes with unobserved features and limited observed links. NODE-CHOOSE significantly outperforms the best-performing GNNs on this new dataset. In the context of large-scale data sets, sparse matrices often play a significant role. A common task involves estimating a low-rank tensor by analyzing a sparse matrix that results from the inner product of two sparse vectors. A crucial application of this is sparse support estimation in regression, where the support is the set of indices of non-zero entries. A recent algorithm, LRT, has been developed to solve this challenge by leveraging low-rank tensor structure, leading to significant improvements in efficiency. Nevertheless, LRT's efficiency heavily relies on the quality of the initial guess provided, which is typically a dense matrix containing non-zero entries at the true support. In this work, we introduce a novel algorithm, ISLET, that addresses this limitation by efficiently estimating the relevant entries of the initial guess, thus allowing for the use of an initial guess that is still more efficient than LRT's approach. Experimental results demonstrate that ISLET's running time is significantly lower than LRT's, while matching or even surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art algorithms. Moreover, ISLET's ability to efficiently estimate initial guesses can be further extended to other applications such as sparse regression with structured support and sparse regression with missing entries. Finally, we have also developed an open-source implementation of ISLET and demonstrated its superiority over existing algorithms. In the context of human-agent team collaboration, accurately grasping the other entity's mental state is essential for seamless communication. To investigate this, we conducted a study in the virtual world of Overcooked 2 with 32 participants who played with an intelligent partner, subject to varying levels of autonomy. Our results revealed that as the autonomy level increased, players' perceptions of their partner's intentions and needs became more stable, but their confidence in these assessments decreased. Furthermore, when the autonomy level was highest, players' perceptions of their partner's intentions were more accurate, but their confidence in these assessments did not improve. Our analysis also showed that players' confidence in their own actions was enhanced at higher autonomy levels, indicating improved self-trust. These findings suggest that as the autonomy level increases, human collaborators become more accurate in reading the agent's mental state, but lose faith in their partner's ability to execute its actions, ultimately leading to a delicate balance in the dynamics of human-agent collaboration. Our study offers valuable insights for the development of more effective human-agent collaboration by highlighting the need to strike a balance between autonomy and collaboration in complex team tasks. Link prediction, a critical component of graph learning, is particularly challenging when limited short-term historical data is available. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called Generalized Connection Learning with Semantic Correlation Recognition (GCSR), which leverages the concept of correlation to enhance link forecasting capabilities. The proposed GCSR framework consists of two key components: a Generalized Connection Learning (GCL) model that captures short-term temporal dependencies, and a Semantic Correlation Recognition (SCR) model that extracts long-term semantic correlations. By integrating these components, GCSR achieves superior performance in link forecasting on real-world datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of GCSR, which outperforms existing methods by a substantial margin in link prediction and ranking tasks. Additionally, our approach can be seamlessly integrated into various graph learning models to improve their performance. A location-based service (LBS) protocol has been developed to ensure user privacy, leveraging edge computing to process and analyze user location data before it reaches the server for analysis. This protocol enables LBS providers to offer services while adhering to user privacy policies. However, the introduction of edge nodes creates potential security risks, specifically for users whose data is being processed by nodes with unverified or unreliable properties. In response, the protocol has been enhanced to incorporate edge node verification, enabling users to assess and validate these nodes before processing and transmitting location data to the server. This verification process is facilitated by a blockchain-based platform that stores edge node information, making it possible for users to retrieve and assess this data in real-time. The protocol's security and efficiency were evaluated through comprehensive simulations and experiments, which revealed that the enhanced protocol significantly reduces the privacy leakage of location data compared to existing approaches. Moreover, the simulations demonstrated that the protocol's efficiency and performance were comparable to that of the baseline approach. Notably, the results showed that the protocol's ability to verify edge nodes resulted in a substantial reduction in privacy leakage, specifically up to 35.7% and 45.1% for different types of attacks, respectively. In terms of overhead, the protocol's edge node verification process resulted in a slight increase in energy consumption, specifically 5% and 6.5% for different types of attacks, although this was still within acceptable limits. This enhanced protocol offers a secure and efficient solution for LBS providers to offer services while safeguarding user privacy. Moreover, the results suggest that the protocol's ability to provide a verifiable edge node service can significantly enhance its security and performance. This is particularly true for edge services that require user trust, such as those providing location data services. In contrast, the results also suggest that the protocol's overhead can be minimized by optimizing the verification process, specifically by only verifying edge nodes that have been compromised in the past. This optimization can be achieved through the use of a reputation system that stores and tracks edge node reputation information, making it possible to identify and verify only those nodes with the lowest reputation and thus minimizing the overhead associated with verifying edge nodes. In this case, the results showed that the optimal number of verified nodes is 3, which resulted in a significant reduction of 35.7% and 45.1% in privacy leakage for different types of attacks, respectively. This is a more efficient approach to verifying edge nodes, and it can be especially useful in scenarios where energy consumption is a major concern.

Moreover, we observe that the proposed T-MFCCs can be learned from a single dataset without requiring pre-trained MFCCs, offering a more efficient and efficient solution. However, we also note that the proposed T-MFCCs can be more computationally expensive than traditional MFCCs. Our research contributes to the development of a new class of features for speaker authentication and speech processing, offering a more efficient and efficient solution. Our aim is to contribute to the ongoing development of speedrunning as a field within the field of interactive video games. Finally, we discuss potential directions for future research in this area. We propose a system to assess the impact of grammatical errors on the overall quality of written content, focusing on a subset of 20 grammatical mistakes considered particularly important by a group of 20 professional writers. Our system evaluates 1.17 million Wikipedia articles and classifies them into three categories: no mistakes, intermediate, and most errors. The results show that articles with grammatical errors are significantly less readable than those without errors, and while both sets of articles are less common in English than in non-Western languages, they are more prevalent among native English speakers. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that grammatical mistakes are often linked to lower reading comprehension. We also explore the relationship between grammatical mistakes and content accuracy, discovering that they can potentially result in more inaccurate information being consumed. Finally, our research suggests that people with limited English proficiency tend to rely more heavily on grammatical corrections to improve their understanding of content. Overall, our findings suggest that while grammatical mistakes are not uncommon, they can have substantial consequences for both readers and writers. The data and source code used in this research are available for public access. The accompanying video also provides a more detailed explanation of our methodology and results. This research investigates the feasibility of using deep learning techniques to optimize a non-orthogonal multiple access downlink system. A custom deep neural network is designed, trained to generate optimal precoding weights in a successive interference elimination framework by mimicking the operations of a conventional algorithm. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this approach yields significant improvements in terms of sum-rate output and energy efficiency compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, this deep neural network-based solution can operate independently of underlying channel characteristics without requiring explicit knowledge or estimation. As a result, it is well-suited for practical applications where channel information might be unavailable or unreliable. To validate the effectiveness of this approach in real-world scenarios, a comparative analysis is performed using simulated channel data generated by popular communication standards, including 5G New Radio and Wi-Fi. These results indicate that the deep neural network exhibits a degree of adaptability to varying channel conditions across different standards. Additionally, it is shown that this deep learning approach can successfully adapt to changes in the number of active users within a network. Overall, this research presents a powerful and efficient learning-based solution for non-orthogonal multiple access downlink systems, capable of delivering improved performance without requiring explicit channel knowledge. A publicly accessible implementation of this approach is available at https://github.com/ArashAsadiJamerani/Non-Orthogonal-Multiple-Access-Deep-Neural-Net. For potential use in a cloud radio access network environment, an optimized implementation of this deep neural network-based non-orthogonal multiple access algorithm is also provided at https://github.com/Neural-Net-AutoTuner/Non-Orthogonal-Multiple-Access-Deep-Neural-Net. This optimized version is specifically designed to run efficiently on Google Colab, thereby facilitating its seamless deployment across different cloud computing platforms. In summary, this research presents a novel, learning-based framework for non-orthogonal multiple access downlink systems, capable of delivering improved performance without requiring explicit channel knowledge. light transmission. Our method employs a single camera to capture images of a display
under various illumination conditions, then utilizes a deep convolutional neural network
to classify the observed pixels and pinpoint dead ones. Our network design incorporates
efficient receptive fields, which have been shown to significantly reduce the number of
required parameters while maintaining a low memory footprint. This allows for the
deployment of our method on devices with limited memory resources, such as smartphones.

a high accuracy rate of 99.1% on a publicly available dataset in a real-world setting. We

We introduce a novel approach to evaluate reinforcement learning policies in a broad range of scenarios, leveraging a model-based approach that utilizes a generative model to simulate agent behavior. Empirical evidence shows that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and data efficiency, and can be applied to a range of reinforcement learning algorithms, including those utilizing novel exploration techniques. This paper introduces a novel indoor video head identification system leveraging
motion-sensitive features. The proposed system overcomes the limitations of conventional
methods, which are ineffective in indoor environments with fixed cameras. The motion-sensitive
features are extracted from a motion estimation network that utilizes optical flow estimation
and a motion-aware loss function. The proposed siamese network architecture, called MPSN,
utilizes motion-sensitive features, resulting in superior performance on indoor video head
identification tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that MPSN surpasses existing methods
by 9.2% in terms of Equal Error Rate and 11.1% in terms of Calibrated Equal Error Rate. Moreover,
our MPSN model achieves comparable performance on indoor speaker verification tasks, even in
adversarial conditions. The model also exhibits adaptability in different deployment scenarios. The
source code of our MPSN model is available for public access on https://github.com/kuangsheng/MPSN. 
Our research marks a pioneering effort in exploring motion-sensitive features for indoor video head
identification tasks. The study also highlights the potential of using motion estimation networks for
extracting relevant features in various computer vision applications.

We propose a novel task for query resolution, called entailing queries, which demands a sequence of steps, often referred to as an entailing chain, to transform an initial premise into an answer statement in a logically sound and coherent manner. The primary advantage of entailing chains is their ability to provide users with detailed explanations for how a statement can be derived. However, current approaches to query resolution often produce chains with errors or inaccuracies, which can undermine users' trust in the system and render their explanations unreliable.

To address these limitations, we present a new framework called Entailer, which is designed to produce entailing chains that respect logical soundness and coherence. The Entailer framework relies on a pre-trained model for query resolution and a set of manually curated rules that assess the validity of entailing chains. We demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods in terms of producing accurate and coherent entailing chains and provide evidence of its superiority in generating chains that users can verify and find convincing. The Entailer code is publicly available for further investigation. This study marks the first instance of a task that necessitates both logical soundness and coherence. The Entailer framework is a pioneering solution that can produce chains with these dual guarantees, paving the way for the development of more advanced query resolution systems. Additionally, specific examples are provided to illustrate unipotent and unramified sections within the context of crystalline cohomology. These examples are constructed as extensions by utilizing the cohomology of perfect fields as a reference framework. Furthermore, this study establishes a connection between unramified and unipotent sections, which is rooted in the unipotent section formula as initially presented by Laumon and Rouquier. This formula is utilized to derive unipotent section formulas for Grothendieck's die Festschrift as well as for the cohomology of local fields, which is characterized by a positive characteristic. Notably, a key component of the formula employed in this study is a spectral sequence that does not possess the properties of a filtration, unlike the standard filtration typically associated with crystalline cohomology. Consequently, a more general definition of the weight filtration is introduced to address this discrepancy. This revised understanding of the weight filtration is shown to be consistent with Grothendieck's initial definition. This connection is utilized to derive a formula for the p-adic Hodge filtration. Lastly, a comparison is made between the weight filtration and the p-adic Hodge filtration. A novel approach combines a Mel-frequency cepstral coefficient levensbergegram transformer with a transformer to analyze the speech of COVID-19 patients and distinguish it from that of patients with other conditions. Furthermore, the model demonstrated exceptional ability to identify acute versus severe distress in COVID-19 patients, reaching 93% and 95% accuracy respectively. These findings suggest that machine learning models can effectively distinguish COVID-19 patients' speech patterns to predict their clinical status. Consequently, this technology has the potential to aid healthcare professionals in early patient screening, reducing hospital admissions, especially for those with severe symptoms. Moreover, this technology can be employed to monitor COVID-19 patients remotely, thus reducing the workload of healthcare professionals. Overall, we believe that this new criterion offers a valuable and versatile tool for assessing conditional independence relationships within graphical models. This study focuses on developing a method to estimate a stochastic process's past states with minimal frequency observations, where the process is governed by a diffusion with unknown parameters. We examine scenarios where the process is observed at times that are randomly spaced according to a given distribution. By creating a novel type of Markov chain, the process can be reconstructed from its past states. Although this approach may not perfectly align with the original diffusion process, it provides a suitable approximation. Our results are applied to a wide range of diffusions, including those with cubic and diffusion-coefficient functions. We also discuss the potential benefits of incorporating a hidden Markov structure within the reconstruction algorithm. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm to estimate the parameters of the observation interval distribution. Our results are supported by numerical simulations. Current image and video restoration techniques excel at restoring damaged images, but their capacity to improve dynamic videos with temporary damage is relatively unexplored. We introduce a new metric called Dynamic Video Repair Capability, or DVRC, which assesses the effectiveness of different image and video restoration methods in repairing dynamic videos. Our research involves analyzing the performance of 20 different restoration techniques on 100 test videos with various types of damage, and we found that while some methods excel at certain types of damage, none surpass all others. Building on these findings, we propose a new combination approach that significantly enhances the DVRC score, and achieves state-of-the-art results on most types of damage. Our work also involves a new dataset of dynamic videos with various types of damage, which is made available for public use. Arabic speech transcription, specifically for the Tunisian dialect, is a complex task due to its unique characteristics and widespread dialectal variations. This study addresses the challenge of transcribing Tunisian Arabizi, a dialect variant, by employing a sequence-to-sequence model that can simultaneously predict multiple levels of transcription: phonemes, words, and characters. To achieve this, the research utilizes the TAA corpus, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 7,000 Tunisian Arabizi audio samples, transcribed at three distinct levels. To overcome limitations in the corpus, the research introduces an innovative data augmentation technique that leverages a sequence-to-sequence model to generate additional training data. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, the study compares the performance of a sequence-to-sequence model with an attention mechanism and an RNN-based sequence-to-sequence model trained with and without the proposed data augmentation method, respectively. Experimental results demonstrate that combining multiple tasks leads to improved transcription accuracy, with an overall character error rate of 24.4%, a significant improvement over the standalone task, with a 4.6% reduction in character error rate. Furthermore, the proposed data augmentation method enhances the performance of the sequence-to-sequence model, with a 2.5% reduction in character error rate, when employed in combination with an attention mechanism, thereby outperforming existing Tunisian Arabizi transcription systems. To facilitate future research, the study's code and dataset will be made publicly available. This research has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of Tunisian Arabizi speech-to-text systems. This distinction supports the idea that these elements were produced during separate, rare events. To address the Z-boson anomaly, certain models propose the existence of a leptophilic gauge boson, which could be a Z-prime boson, accompanied by a Z-4 boson with a 4 TeV mass. This research explores the feasibility of detecting such particles at facilities utilizing discarded lepton colliders in the energy range of 0.5 TeV to 4 TeV, the PIP-II at 20 GeV, and KEKB at 5 GeV, with a focus on their interactions with electrons and muons. A simplified framework for the interactions is applied, and the results indicate that the ILC and PIP-II have the capability to detect these particles, even with limited integrated luminosity, while KEVB and BEPC-II have lower detection prospects. This research also considers the background from lepton pair production and the potential for utilizing discarded colliders to narrow down the mass range of the new bosons, ultimately contributing to identifying the underlying new physics. A detailed analysis of the experimental setup and the expected detection efficiency is provided, along with a discussion of the implications of the experimental results on the model parameters. This research demonstrates that the detection of the Z-prime boson can be achieved through the observation of the following: (i) PIP-II observing a Z-prime boson mass of 2.5 TeV with a cross-section of 0.5 fb, 20 fb^-1 luminosity, and a 5-sigma significance level; (ii) ILC observing a Z-prime boson mass of 2.5 TeV with a 0.5 fb cross-section, 1 fb^-1 luminosity, and a 5-sigma significance level; (iii) PIP-II observing a Z-4 boson mass of 3.0 TeV with a 0.5 fb cross-section, 20 fb^-1 luminosity, and a 5-sigma significance level; (iv) ILC observing a Z-4 boson mass of 3.0 TeV with a 0.5 fb cross-section, 1 fb^-1 luminosity, and a 5-sigma significance level; (v) KEVB observing a Z-4 boson mass of 2.0 TeV with a 0.5 fb cross-section, 1 fb^-1 luminosity, and a 5-sigma significance level; (vi) BEPC-II observing a Z-4 boson mass of 2.

The next decade will see a significant surge in dark energy investigations, thanks to the launch of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and the forthcoming operational status of the Euclid, DESI, and Simons Observatory projects. These initiatives will provide a vast amount of data for precise measurements of the dark universe. However, the full potential of this data will only be realized when combined with other observational programs. This report identifies key areas where additional observational efforts are necessary to maximize the impact of these flagship investigations and proposes potential future observational projects to achieve this goal. These projects will complement existing initiatives and enhance our understanding of the universe. Specifically, the projects listed comprise two categories: Type 1, core investigations that are crucial to achieving the flagship projects' full potential, and Type 2, specialized projects that will significantly contribute to the field. This report highlights the importance of these projects and provides a roadmap for their implementation. It also includes a list of recommended projects for the next decade, which will be formalized through the Cosmic Visions document. These projects are designed to be feasible, particularly in the next decade, and to facilitate their implementation, this document provides a summary of the necessary facilities and observational strategies required to achieve the projects' goals. Furthermore, it outlines the necessary collaborations and international partnerships needed to ensure their success. This report is an official submission to the 2021 Snowmass study on the future of the cosmic frontier. Its contents are based on input from various experts and are intended to provide a comprehensive overview of the projects listed. This report is meant to serve as a starting point for further discussion and development, and its goals are to facilitate the next decade's scientific endeavors. This document will be updated periodically to reflect any changes to the projects listed, and a revised version will be submitted to the Cosmic Visions working group. A novel approach is presented to efficiently assess the energy performance of RC shear walls under earthquake-induced damage. A trained artificial neural network, specifically a hybrid model combining long short-term memory and multilayer perceptron techniques, predicts the energy dissipation capacity of RC shear walls, taking into account various design and earthquake-related factors. The proposed model is trained using data from over 100,000 simulations and validated using experimental data from 36 tests on model shear tests. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in predicting the energy dissipation capacity, with a notable accuracy of 95%, and highlight its potential to be applied to other structural elements like columns and beams. The use of this approach in high-throughput design optimization is also demonstrated, yielding significant design improvements in under 15 minutes. The optimized designs outperform conventional ones, with a 12% increase in capacity and a 18% reduction in demand. The impact of seismic activity on structural performance is also discussed, with a case study illustrating the effects of seismic activity on energy demands. Ultimately, the proposed method is envisioned to be integrated into automated design tools, enabling rapid and efficient design optimization under seismic activity. In the field of particle physics, real-time event data analysis is crucial for selection and filtering processes. Event data analysis heavily relies on particle reconstruction techniques, particularly those using neural networks, which are computationally intensive. Recent advancements in FPGAs have made it possible to deploy neural networks in real-time, but their application in graph neural networks has been limited until now. This study presents a novel method for efficiently implementing graph neural networks on FPGAs and evaluates its performance in real-time particle reconstruction. By comparing our approach with existing state-of-the-art methods, we demonstrate that our technique yields comparable results while significantly reducing runtime and improving scalability. Additionally, we provide a detailed case study of real-time particle reconstruction and suggest future research directions to further accelerate graph neural networks on FPGAs. In the field of cardiovascular disease diagnosis, analyzing coronary artery calcium (CAC) is a fundamental step. The process of quantifying CAC is complex, as it involves detecting and outlining calcified coronary plaque areas within CT images. The majority of existing methods for this task are based on deep neural networks that learn from data, but their underlying processes are not always transparent. This lack of transparency hampers the ability to re-create or verify results, and is particularly problematic in critical medical applications. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages generative adversarial networks to derive a differentiable mapping between original CT image intensity values and CAC volume measurements. This approach enables us to train a model that can accurately quantify CAC volumes while providing fine-grained control over intensity values. The resulting model exhibits superior performance compared to conventional methods, achieving a 95.0% volume Dice score and 87.1% percentage error on a dataset of 1,000 images. The associated code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/AndrzejJurowski/CAC-GAN. To ensure reproducibility, we provide a detailed report of our method, including the data, models, and experimental setup used. The supplementary materials, including pre-trained models, are hosted on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4500620. Our work is the first to provide a generative model for CAC quantification, and is a significant step towards achieving transparency in this field. A discrete form of the Boltzmann equation is formulated for simulating plasma shock waves, which then serves as the basis for a particle simulation method. This method's accuracy is examined through two assessments: the first, being the Chandrasekhara measure, and the second, being the kinetic balance, both of which are crucial for verifying the proposed model's validity. Results from these assessments indicate that the developed model is accurate. Spiking neural networks have gained popularity due to their ability to mimic biological processes and efficient communication via event-driven spikes. The use of surrogate gradients has been a common training method in SNNs, which is based on modified gradient descent. However, SNN training is notoriously challenging due to the non-differentiable nature of surrogate gradients. To address this issue, we propose a novel training pipeline that incorporates regularization and standardization techniques. Through our experiments, which involved applying surrogate gradient descent to SNNs on three complex classification tasks, we demonstrated that the proposed pipeline significantly enhances the performance of SNNs, achieving up to a 30% improvement in accuracy compared to baseline models. Furthermore, we found that the regularization and standardization techniques can be effectively applied to SNNs without compromising their energy efficiency. The resulting models not only outperform state-of-the-art SNNs but also surpass traditional artificial neural networks in terms of accuracy and energy efficiency. Overall, our findings suggest that the use of regularization and standardization techniques can be a powerful approach for training non-sparse SNNs, which is essential for their practical application in real-world systems. In a competitive environment, individuals sharing their predictions may have to sacrifice their accuracy due to privacy concerns, leading to an inferior aggregate outcome. To address this issue, we explore a new approach that strikes a balance between privacy and performance, using a novel metric called the mean squared error rate. This metric takes into account both the quality of predictions and the degree of privacy. We then develop an optimal method for allocating weights to predictions that maximizes the private forecasting outcome while adhering to performance constraints. Interestingly, our results indicate that under certain conditions, optimal private predictions remain optimal even when the constraints are relaxed, allowing for improved outcomes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in a competitive setting, predictions tend to converge towards the optimal private metric as more predictors are taken into account, assuming they are truthful about their performance. However, in a cooperative environment, achieving the optimal private performance is contingent upon the number of predictors involved. Specifically, our analysis reveals that if all predictors contribute, they can achieve the optimal private performance. Nevertheless, if only a single predictor is involved, they can only approximate this optimal performance. To validate our theoretical findings, we conduct an experiment where individuals are randomly assigned to provide predictions, thereby minimizing the risk of biased outcomes. This study focuses on the application of pre-trained language models to infer traceability paths in software engineering. The authors also discuss the potential implications of their work for future research in automated software engineering.

The 3D graph neural network has become a preferred method for analyzing molecular properties due to its ability to process complex molecular structures. However, traditional 3D GNNs have significant limitations stemming from their reliance on predefined topological structures and lack of generalizability across various molecular representations. To overcome these challenges, a novel 3D equivariant graph network, called the Equiformer, has been developed. By integrating a self-attention mechanism with a message passing paradigm, the Equiformer enables the simultaneous learning of molecular representations and prediction of molecular properties. Utilizing learned molecular embeddings, the Equiformer can accurately represent molecules in 3D space and efficiently compute interatomic distances. Through extensive testing on multiple datasets, the Equiformer has demonstrated superior performance in predicting molecular properties compared to current state-of-the-art models. Notably, the Equiformer has achieved a new record in regression tasks, with a 10% improvement in RMSE on the ZINC dataset and a 20% improvement in MAE on the QM9 dataset. Furthermore, the Equiformer has shown exceptional performance in quantum-chemical regression tasks, with a 10% improvement in RMSE on the dataset. Additionally, the Equiformer has been successfully applied to the challenging task of predicting molecular energy and enthalpy, with a 10% improvement in MAE on the QM9 dataset. Overall, the Equiformer has established a new benchmark for the 3D GNN community, with a strong potential for future advancements in molecular representation learning and property prediction. This innovative approach utilizes a parameterized quantum circuit to generate a parameter-dependent Gaussian state, and a classical optimization process to identify the optimal parameter configuration that corresponds to the highest target binding affinity. The versatility of the GBF model allows for seamless adaptation to a wide array of target systems, making it an attractive option for medication discovery applications. In this study, we successfully apply the GBF model to a well-established anti-cancer target system, demonstrating its ability to efficiently explore large binding affinity spaces and identify high-potential systems. Our results show that the GBF model can accurately predict binding affinities within a 1 order-of-magnitude margin of error, highlighting the potential of the GBF framework in the context of large-scale medication discovery. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability of the GBF model to identify high-potential systems that exhibit significantly higher binding affinities than the existing standard-of-care compound. These findings suggest that the GBF model has the potential to revolutionize the medication discovery process, enabling rapid and efficient exploration of vast chemical search spaces with unprecedented accuracy and performance. Our work paves the way for the development of a fully programmable GBF-based system that can be applied to a wide array of target systems, laying the foundation for future breakthroughs in the field of medication discovery. Natural Language Understanding, a field of artificial intelligence, has long been a subject of research. Recently, a resurgence in Natural Language Processing has led to significant breakthroughs in Natural Language Generation, with Natural Language Generation Systems now being applied in areas such as customer support, content creation, and information retrieval. This work focuses on developing a Natural Language Generation System specifically for the legal field, where it will serve as a component of a system capable of automatically producing contracts. Ultimately, this system will enable non-legal professionals to receive draft contracts, accompanied by an explanation of the agreement. Our research presents a Natural Language Generation framework tailored to this objective, along with preliminary results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the system on a limited dataset. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and difficulties encountered in developing an NLG system for the legal domain, highlighting the need for more comprehensive training data to achieve optimal results. To address this issue, we propose a strategy to expand our dataset, drawing from the legal expertise of practicing attorneys. Our long-term goal is to acquire a substantial amount of data, enabling the development of a robust Natural Language Generation System capable of producing high-quality draft contracts for common legal transactions. This paper serves as a preliminary study, outlining the project's objectives, current achievements, and potential avenues for future research. It is our intention to continue refining and updating this paper as our progress advances. Recent advances in image-to-image translation and image separation tasks have led to the development of image separation networks. These models, however, are typically trained using paired data which can be difficult to obtain, limiting their practicality. This paper introduces a Semi-Supervised StyleGAN approach to the image separation task, enabling unpaired data to be used for training. By leveraging the stylegan architecture, we are able to leverage its pre-trained generator for superior image quality and its discriminator for guidance during training. This allows us to train our network without a pre-trained network, and instead utilize a novel semi-supervised loss function that incorporates both supervised and unsupervised elements. This loss function leverages the discriminator's ability to identify separated images, and image relationships through a novel triplet loss extension. This enables our network to be trained using unpaired data, and ultimately results in high-quality image separation results. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming existing state-of-the-art image separation methods. This work is the first to apply the stylegan architecture to the image separation task, and is open-sourced at https://github.com/OranGerard/semi_stylegan. To boost inference performance, hybrid DNN accelerators combine CMOS cores with 3D memristors to lower latency and energy consumption. However, the high number of interactions between the cores and memristors generates significant traffic within the network, which can become a major bottleneck. To address this issue, we introduce ENOS, an energy-efficient network architecture designed to minimize network latency and energy consumption. ENOS leverages a novel search algorithm to optimize network administrator placement and routing strategies, thereby reducing network traffic and alleviating network congestion. To further minimize energy consumption, ENOS employs a dynamic programming algorithm to develop an energy-efficient routing solution. We define and examine a stochastic representation of a symmetric matrix, 
referenced as stage set uniform ellipticity, and establish its equivalent to the 
existing partial uniform ellipticity concept. Additionally, we explore its utility 
in designing a tailored algorithm for the $L_2$ gradient method. This new 
representation enables more precise control over the volume expansion and 
contraction properties of the map in question. This understanding is leveraged to 
develop a modified algorithm that converges in at most the same number of 
iterations as traditional methods, yet with the advantage of a potentially much 
smaller initial step size. This innovation enables a more efficient approach 
especially suited to the highly non-smooth, high-dimensional scenarios. Finally, 
we demonstrate this novel method's utility in solving a class of matrix-compressed 
Hamilton-Jacobi equations. The results are validated through numerical experiments. 
The accompanying code is also provided.

discrete Hamilton--Jacobi equations and the $L^2$ algorithm". 
This revised version incorporates an additional section on the theory of measure 
theory, stage set theory, and graph theory, as well as a new section on the 
algorithm for the $L^2$ gradient method.

The precise measurement of the Higgs self-coupling is a crucial aspect of the Higgs precision physics program, requiring the combination of individual measurements to achieve high accuracy. This study focuses on the current status and future potential of determining the Higgs self-coupling through colliders, specifically highlighting the unique capabilities of lepton colliders. By analyzing the combined results of current and future experiments globally, we assess the potential for improvement in measuring the Higgs self-coupling and find that a combined uncertainty of less than 10% can be achieved. This outcome underscores the importance of current and future lepton collider initiatives in advancing Higgs precision physics. Additionally, we investigate the combined result's sensitivity to various factors, including the correlation of individual measurements, and demonstrate that a future global combined result will be relatively stable despite changes in experimental parameters. This study also considers the impact of theoretical model assumptions on the combined result, revealing that a deviation from the standard model can be detected with a significance of 1.5σ even under different theoretical scenarios. Ultimately, we conclude that a future global combined result will be highly effective in revealing any deviations from the standard model. In complex environments where interactions are unpredictable, agents must develop strategies that work despite uncertainty. This uncertainty can lead to multiple agents learning in isolation, which can negatively impact teamwork. In such situations, we propose that effective collaboration requires agents to find satisfactory solutions that work despite uncertainty. This approach, called satisficing, can significantly improve collaboration in unpredictable environments. We developed an algorithm that uses a cost-benefit analysis to find satisfactory solutions that are robust to uncertainty, outperforming existing methods in competitive zero-sum games and stochastic games. This approach, called RobustSatisficing, can be used in conjunction with reinforcement learning to improve collaborative performance in unpredictable environments. This work highlights the importance of finding satisfactory solutions that are robust to uncertainty, which can greatly enhance collaborative performance in complex environments. field with a novel regularization technique, our method can produce high-
quality, detailed images with varying levels of brightness. Our results demonstrate
that SBFNet outperforms existing techniques in terms of visual quality and
performance. Additionally, we show that SBFNet's shading fields can be used to
enhance portrait images by simulating natural lighting effects. Notably, our
method can also be used to synthesize images with realistic shading and
texturing, allowing for a more nuanced and detailed portrait image. Our code

The real-time simulation of fission dynamics in actinides is studied using a time-dependent mean-field framework, which incorporates the dissipation of energy into the quadrupole collective motion. This is achieved by introducing a coupling between the collective and quasiparticle degrees of freedom, which is modeled as a coupling strength and range. The effects of varying these parameters are explored, with a focus on their impact on dissipation in fission. Key metrics such as dissipation per unit time and the dissipation force are calculated and analyzed. Notably, the results show that the dissipation force is highly dependent on the coupling parameters, while the dissipation rate is more robust against changes in these parameters. Furthermore, the study reveals that the dissipation mechanism is primarily responsible for the fission barrier's weakening as the system approaches fission. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the role of dissipation in fission and its relationship with the parameters governing the coupling between the quasiparticle and collective degrees of freedom. As robots and autonomous systems increasingly integrate into our daily lives, ensuring their safety is a top priority. Researchers have developed "safety overseers" to monitor and regulate these systems in critical situations, but the effectiveness of current methods in training overseers is still unclear. To address this gap, we conducted a comprehensive comparison of various training techniques for overseers, examining five different approaches in depth. Our analysis revealed that two methods, NARX-LSTM and Memory Network, consistently outperformed the others, but the most critical finding is that the training process for overseers is highly sensitive to changes in system dynamics. To mitigate this vulnerability, we introduced a hybrid training method that leverages advanced techniques like data augmentation and generative adversarial networks, enabling the development of more robust and effective safety overseers. Ultimately, we provide a set of guidelines and recommendations to enhance future research in this area. Finally, we apply our findings to a real-world scenario, demonstrating the potential of our top-performing oversee in a critical system failure. A new concept in quantum heat engines, known as the interaction-amplified quantum heat engine (IAQHE), has been proposed and analyzed.  This novel engine, which utilizes an interacting quantum gas as its working substance, can significantly boost the heat supply.  Unlike traditional quantum heat engines, the IAQHE leverages the interactions between particles to increase the heat supply, thereby enabling the working substance to absorb more heat from the hot reservoir.  As a result, the required temperature difference between the hot and cold reservoirs can be minimized.  This study introduces the groundbreaking principles of the IAQHE and demonstrates its enhanced efficiency through both analytical and numerical approaches.  Furthermore, the research explores the impact of various parameters, such as temperature, interaction strength, and particle numbers, on the performance of the IAQHE.  Ultimately, the findings of this study are expected to inspire further advancements in the field of quantum heat engines. This research develops a multivariate extension of the Functional Singular Spectrum Method (FSST) to analyze complex high-dimensional data. The proposed approach, named Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Evaluation (Mult-FSSE), can handle data sets with any number of features. It's demonstrated that Mult-FSSE outperforms existing techniques when dealing with high-dimensional data, especially when analyzing features with the same dimensionality. Furthermore, the method can efficiently extract relevant information from data sets with different dimensionalities. To validate these claims, simulations and real-world data applications are employed. Additionally, the method's ability to handle noisy data and the computational efficiency of its components are evaluated. The proposed Mult-FSSE approach is then applied to analyze gene expression data from cancer patients, providing insights into the diverse characteristics of different cancer types. The accompanying appendix includes a MATLAB implementation of the method.

Self-supervised learning's recent advancements have been notable, particularly with the introduction of multiple contrastive learning methods. Notably, these methods have shown promising results in various tasks, yet they are heavily dependent on the quality of training data. In this paper, we aim to investigate the impact of dataset inaccuracies on self-supervised learning methods. Our investigation reveals that the contrastive loss is highly susceptible to inaccuracies in the dataset, leading to a decline in its generalization capabilities. In response, we propose an alternative loss function, grounded in the principles of maximum entropy, to enhance robustness against dataset inaccuracies. Our proposed method, which we term maximum entropy contrastive learning, demonstrates superior resilience to dataset inaccurities, outperforming its contrastive counterpart in various evaluations. We also examine the effect of model pretraining on the results and find that the presence of inaccuracies in the dataset can negatively impact the model's quality. In contrast, the proposed method yields a more resilient pre-trained model. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the dataset inaccuracies problem and offers a more robust and resilient approach to self-supervised learning. In brain neoplasm segmentation, where multiple imaging modalities are available, researchers have been exploring methods to combine them for more accurate results. Existing approaches often rely on specific rules or mathematical calculations to integrate the modalities, but these methods can struggle with discrepancies in image quality and sensitivity. To address this challenge, a new technique is proposed, which involves training a network to generate images for unseen patients, then using these generated images with available ones to enable multi-modal fusion without relying on specific rules. To further enhance performance, a two-tier attention mechanism is applied to selectively focus on the most useful image information. Experimental results on three brain neoplasm segmentation datasets demonstrate that this approach outperforms previous methods, achieving significant improvements in accuracy. Additionally, a study on the impact of quality differences between image modalities shows that this approach can still produce good results even when one modality is of lower quality. The MARSS framework in the R package MARSS relies on a hierarchical Bayesian approach to estimate time-varying parameters in linear dynamic models. This includes state variance components, key parameters, and local shrinkage factors, all of which are essential for model convergence. Calculating standardized residuals, a common practice in regression modeling, can be challenging in the MARSS framework due to the inherent uncertainty in key parameters and local shrinkage factors. This is because the standardization typically involves dividing residuals by standard deviations derived from maximum likelihood estimates of model parameters. This process is problematic because it neglects the uncertainty associated with time-varying parameters and local shrinkage factors. This paper presents a method for computing standardized residuals that takes into account the uncertainty related to time-varying parameters and local shrinkage factors, allowing for more accurate and informative residuals. A simulation study demonstrates the importance of considering parameter uncertainty when computing standardized residuals, showing that neglecting it can lead to misleading results. This approach is applied to real-world data, specifically the US macroeconomic model, illustrating the benefits of considering parameter uncertainty when computing standardized residuals. The results suggest that ignoring this uncertainty can lead to overconfidence in model fit and misleading inferences. The MARSS R package implements the proposed method for calculating standardized residuals. The code and data used in this study are provided in the supplementary materials. This work is an extension of a previous study on the MARSS package, originally presented at the 2021 Joint Statistical Meetings. Extracting structured data from unorganized text has been a significant focus in natural language processing. Current techniques for open domain data extraction rely on either rule-based systems or machine learning models, but not a combination of both. We introduce Graphene, a novel open domain open data extraction system, which integrates the benefits of rule-based extraction and machine learning models. The conventional wisdom in machine learning suggests a balance between a model's precision and robustness cannot be achieved without compromising one or the other. However, this paper argues that traditional machine learning methods may not directly translate to real-world robot learning due to significant differences in how these models interact with their environments. In particular, real-world robot learning environments are highly dynamic and prone to human error, making it difficult to separate model inaccuracies from inaccuracies caused by human mistakes. Based on this analysis, this paper identifies three key factors that contribute to a "hostile" trade-off between robustness and precision in robot learning and proposes a new approach to mitigate its effects. The proposed method combines the use of probabilistic models with a data collection strategy that involves intentionally selecting and introducing noisy data to a robot learning system. The proposed method was tested in a series of experiments involving a robot that learns to navigate obstacles and interact with objects, and the results demonstrate the importance of considering the unique characteristics of robot learning environments in designing learning algorithms. To address the underrepresentation of Chinese characters in video and speech recognition, researchers are turning to multimodal pre-training techniques that leverage Chinese language and video characteristics. However, current pre-training methods are limited by their reliance on cross-modal alignment, which can be compromised when tasks involve mismatched modalities. A proposed pre-training approach, called Contrastive Multimodal Pre-training (CMP), instead focuses on learning from cross-modal contrasts. By capitalizing on the differences between modalities, CMP enables the development of more effective video and language understanding applications, including video captioning and question answering. CMP's pre-training stage involves generating contrastive pairs of video and language segments, which are then used to learn representations that can capture both high-level semantic information and low-level visual and acoustic details. In the downstream task stage, CMP's fine-tuning process utilizes a two-stream architecture that combines visual and linguistic features to generate high-quality results. CMP's effectiveness is demonstrated through superior performance on multiple benchmarks, including the TVQA and VQG tasks. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of several state-of-the-art salient object detection methods, yet most of these methods rely heavily on manually annotated saliency masks, which are time-consuming to obtain. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a novel approach called Saliency Object Counting (SOC). By leveraging object counting techniques, SOC can simultaneously estimate both pixel-level and instance-level saliency maps without requiring explicit annotation. Specifically, SOC first generates a coarse pixel-level saliency map through a weakly-supervised network, and then uses this map to guide a fully-supervised instance detection network, resulting in refined saliency maps. Experimental results on five public salient object detection datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SOC in achieving comparable performance to top-tier fully-supervised methods. Moreover, SOC has shown a significant advantage in terms of speed, being up to 40 times faster than its fully-supervised counterparts. We introduce ViT-BEVSeg, a transformer-based network that leverages a novel bird's eye view representation and efficient hierarchical encoding to tackle the complex task of aerial scene segmentation. By transforming 2D images into their respective BEV representations, we uncover a deeper connection between driving behaviors and aerial scene characteristics. This innovative approach enables the efficient modeling of intricate relationships between driving scenarios and aerial scene properties. Our proposed network comprises two key components: the hierarchical encoder, which rapidly processes aerial images, and the multi-modal transformer, which extracts rich contextual information from the BEV representation. Extensive experimentation demonstrates the superior performance of ViT-BEVSeg, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin on the Sim10K dataset. Furthermore, our method excels in terms of efficiency, utilizing a mere 1.5% GPU memory and a 20ms inference time per image, making it an attractive solution for real-time applications.
